title: Kafka's Metamorphosis
objective: After this level you can weigh two readings of Kafka's story of a man who wakes up as an insect.
summary: In Kafka's Die Verwandlung (1915), Gregor Samsa wakes as a monstrous vermin and worries about work. Readers weigh two readings: a family story and a story about dehumanizing labor.

cards.headline: A salesman wakes up as a giant insect. His first worry? Being late.
cards.body: Franz Kafka's story, first published in German in 1915, opens with Gregor Samsa, a traveling salesman, changed in his bed into a gigantic insect. Before panic, before horror, his mind goes to work and his demanding boss. What kind of story starts like that?

cards.headline: Changed, but into what?
cards.body: Kafka called it Die Verwandlung, "the transformation." He had translated part of Ovid's Metamorphoses at school, yet he didn't borrow Ovid's title. His first sentence calls Gregor an "ungeheueren Ungeziefer", roughly a monstrous vermin, and he kept the creature's exact kind vague. He even told his publisher the insect must not be drawn on the cover, not even from a distance.

cards.headline: Reading 1: the family
cards.body: Gregor is his family's sole provider. Once he changes, their response moves from shock to rejection, and his sister, who first cares for him, finally insists they must get rid of the monster. Kafka's own father was a domineering businessman. In 1919 Kafka wrote him a long letter he never sent, and Britannica says it reveals the background to the father-son conflict in many of his stories.

cards.headline: Reading 2: the job
cards.body: Look at what Gregor thinks about first. He frets that he has missed the five o'clock train, and the next leaves at seven. Scholars read the story through several lenses, and one is the dehumanizing effects of labor. On that reading, the insect makes visible what the job had already done to him: he was valued for what he earned.

mascot.line: You don't have to pick one reading. Ask which clues each one explains best, then weigh them.

cards.headline: Kafka: weighed
learned: Gregor's creature is kept deliberately vague
Reading 1: the family and Kafka's father
Reading 2: work that makes a man a thing

questions.prompt: The German title Kafka chose, Die Verwandlung, means _____.

options.label: the insect
options.rationale: Kafka kept the creature out of the title, and off the cover.

options.label: the salesman
options.rationale: Gregor is one, but that's not the title.

options.label: the family
options.rationale: The family matters, but the title names the change.

questions.explanation: Die Verwandlung means the transformation. Kafka knew Ovid's Metamorphoses but chose his own German word.

questions.prompt: Match each name or phrase from Kafka's story with what goes with it.
questions.explanation: Die Verwandlung means the transformation, and ungeheueren Ungeziefer is roughly a monstrous vermin. Gregor Samsa is a traveling salesman, and Kafka's own father was a domineering businessman.

questions.prompt: Kafka had translated part of Ovid at school. Why would Ovid's title have suited his story too (Level 7)?

options.label: Ovid's poem is set in a salesman's family home
options.rationale: Ovid's myths run from creation to Julius Caesar.

options.label: Every story in Ovid's poem involves a transformation
Ovid's poem is about a man who becomes an insect
options.rationale: Daphne becomes a laurel; there's no Gregor in Ovid.

options.label: Ovid banned drawings of his characters
options.rationale: That was Kafka's request about his cover.

questions.explanation: Metamorphoses means transformations, and a change of form plays a part in every one of Ovid's myths. Kafka's title means the same thing in German.
